extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of communication and media studies (academic readers interested in communication theory)
extracted.subtask_description: An academic/theoretical treatment distinguishing two central conceptions of communication (the transmission view and the ritual view), offering a symbolic/cultural approach to analyzing media (especially newspapers) and proposing research questions and ethical considerations for communication studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission view of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined by terms such as 'imparting,' 'sending,' 'transmitting,' or 'giving information to others'; formed from a metaphor of geography or transportation; center is the transmission of signals or messages over distance for the purpose of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically linked to transportation metaphors (telegraph, print, messenger). Use this view to analyze distribution, speed, and control of messages; ask about effects on audiences, dissemination, and the political/economic functions of the medium. Note the religious origins recast in secular/technical terms and the tendency to treat communication as a process of information transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual view of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Linked to 'sharing,' 'participation,' 'association,' 'fellowship,' and 'the possession of a common faith.' Directed toward the maintenance of society in time; communication as representation of shared beliefs rather than mere information transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat communications (e.g., reading a newspaper) as ritual acts or ceremonies that 'portray' and 'confirm' a social order. Focus on participation, communal affirmation, dramatization of social roles, and the maintenance/renewal of cultural meanings rather than on transmission or effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze newspapers as transmission instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a transmission view the newspaper is seen as an instrument for disseminating news and knowledge over larger distances; analysis centers on information effects and functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Does news enlighten or obscure? Does it change or harden attitudes? Does it maintain integration or promote instability? Consider mechanical/behavioral questions of effects, credibility, attitude change, and the newspaper's role in information distribution and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze newspapers as ritual/dramatic texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a ritual view reading a newspaper is like attending a mass: less about learning new information and more about accepting a portrayed view of the world and confirming membership in social roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine presentation, dramatic framing, role-taking invited by stories, and how the paper portrays contending forces. Consider news as historic/cultural form invented by a class (middle class) with particular 'hunger for experience' (novelty), and treat the paper as a cultural performance that gives life order and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication as symbolic process (produce/maintain/repair/transform reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication is 'a symbolic process whereby reality is produced, maintained, repaired, and transformed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center analyses on how symbolic forms create the realities people inhabit rather than treating communication as merely secondary to a preexisting reality. Investigate processes of production, maintenance, repair (handling anomalies), and transformation (paradigm shifts) of shared realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of symbolic forms: displacement and productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic forms possess displacement (speak about things not present) and productivity (finite elements yield infinite representations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these properties to evaluate maps, language, ritual, art, and other symbol systems: how they represent absent things and how productive combinatory rules generate varied realities. Examples: maps, poems, dances as alternative 'modes' of mapping space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols as 'of' and 'for' reality (dual capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic forms operate both as 'symbols of' (representing reality) and 'symbols for' (creating or guiding reality under their direction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating communicative artifacts, assess both their representational function and their performative/constitutive function. Example: a blueprint can be pointed to as a representation, and under its guidance a house is produced (it both describes and constructs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought as public and social (maps/models of environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is predominantly public and social; it consists in constructing maps/models (blackboards, rituals, poems) that allow thought to run models faster than the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cognitive and communicative practices by examining their publicly shared symbolic resources and model-building activities. Example pedagogical or research focus: how public maps enable planning, testing, and social coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of communication are representations 'of' and 'for' communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Models not only describe communication but also guide and produce the communicative behaviors and institutions they represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be reflexive: assess the ethical and social consequences of favoring particular models (e.g., power or anxiety models). Recognize that theoretical models shape policy, institutional practices, and people's motives in ways that may realize the model's assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power and anxiety as reductive models in American social science
rubrics_metrics.description: American social science has often represented communication in terms of power (information theory, learning, influence) or anxiety (dissonance, balance, uses and gratifications), reducing communicative diversity to pursuit of power or flight from anxiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to critique theoretical frameworks that over-simplify motives and to search for broader models (including ritual) that capture aesthetic, religious, and value-sharing dimensions of social life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research agenda/questions for communication studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should ask: How do we create, apprehend, and use significant symbolic forms? What are the differences between art, science, journalism, religion, common sense, mythology? What are historical and comparative variations? How do changes in communication technology influence what we can create and apprehend? How do groups struggle over the definition of what is real?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these guiding questions as evaluative criteria when designing studies or assessing scholarship: breadth (comparative/historical), attention to symbolic form differences, technology's impact on symbolic production, and power struggles over reality construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical reflexivity: models carry ethical implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Because communication models operate 'for' communication as well as 'of' it, they have differing ethical implications and produce different forms of social relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate not just empirical adequacy but ethical and social consequences of models. Ask how adopting a given model (transmission vs ritual, power-centric vs ritual-centric) will shape institutions, practices, and normative outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative prescription: recast studies toward ritual model to restore cultural value
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of recasting studies in terms of a ritual model is to better grasp communication and to rebuild a model of and for communication of restorative value in reshaping common culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing reforms or interventions (in education, urban design, technology policy), evaluate alternatives by whether they expand people's powers to learn/exchange experience and restore ritual/communal dimensions rather than solely serving political/economic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate communication technologies for broader civic/learning ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating each new communication technology solely as opportunity for politics and economics; instead consider opportunities to expand powers to learn and exchange ideas and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technologies by multiple criteria: political/economic uses, but also educational, communal, ritual, and cultural potentials. Critique narrow designs/incentives that prioritize control, trade, or therapy over shared cultural enrichment.
